text: Okay, good morning, everybody.
So congratulations on making the 8:30 slot on the last day of the
conference. I have to say, I sometimes don't make this slot, so well done.
So I want to start really with some really big questions.
So things like how do we move data to
evidence to action and do this at really big
scale? How do we do this with a constantly evolving
dataset where there's new records coming, maybe 10,000,
20,000 records a day, sometimes even an hour, as we move towards
more automated monitoring?
How do we do this with a constantly evolving set of
questions that we have for that data, that sometimes we can't
predict, sometimes with real urgency with which we need
to answer those questions?
How do we do this with provenance so that we can see the
attribution chain as that data moves from that foundational
level
right the way through to synthesis and action with that
data?
And of course, perhaps critically, how do we do this sustainably?
And I mean that across all the different dimensions of sustainability.
So not just ethical sustainability and sort of green sustainability, but
also financial sustainability. And we've seen in
this conference over the past few days, some real challenges
with how we sustain our community and our infrastructures
financially. So tackling these kind of questions, in my
view, these are probably some of the biggest questions that we've got in the
discipline, and this needs some really big thinking.
And fortunately, again, we've seen a number of fantastic sessions throughout
the week that are really trying to tackle this.
And when we, within the Natural History Museum first started to think about this,
we really started to think about,
well, what would be the kind of infrastructures that would
actually solve these kind of problems?
And obviously,
AI, and particularly machine learning, is utterly transforming
our landscape in terms of how we approach answering these
questions. So we've got enormous
examples again this week of how machine learning is extracting
information,
and spotting trends in our data, and then how
large language models are beginning to make inference and link that
data up in ways that truly were unimaginable.
And I think the big thing for me is simply the scale, the
ambition by which we can now have for our data has
truly transformed. And again, for those of you who've come to TADWIG over
regular years, probably the last three years has seen
more innovation in this space than perhaps the last 10.
And that's really because AI is utterly transforming
this landscape So a few years ago now, we started to think,
well, how could we bring this story together?
How could we bring that enormous totality of all that
fragmented data across these huge repositories, and
what would be the kind of infrastructure that we might need to
build to solve these problems? And we had this rather
crazy dream with this insanely ambitious title, A
Planetary Knowledge Base, to bring that story
together. And very crudely, various iterations of this slide have
existed over the past few years, but this is essentially the
sum, if you like, totality of that vision.
Which is how we take our big data infrastructures holding
information about people, observations, collections,
institutions,
genetic data, literature. How do we align all of
that data? What AI tooling will we need to basically connect
that data up? And at the time when we first were thinking about this, we were
heavily invested in knowledge graphs, and indeed still are.
But also we've got foundation models now, and
these large language models derive from those foundation models, which are
allowing us to integrate and synthesize that knowledge and
basically potentially reason statistically across them.
But also then we've got this enormous capability to start to
build services off the back of all of that
enormous data. But the scale of this is
truly intimidating. The sheer volume of data, the
sheer compute capacity, the size of some of these graphs
is truly scary. So one of our challenges was
how do we chunk this problem up into
manageable projects that we could actually start to deliver real
value,
but do this in a way that at the same time started to tackle what we think
is this big, overarching architecture that solves these really
big,
visionary global challenges. And in effect, we broke
this problem up into a series of phases, and we're very much at
phase one. So this is still very much an emerging infrastructure.
But we broke it up into a series of projects that started to tackle
some really profound issues for things like the Biodiversity
Heritage Library, for digitization, and also something I'll come on
to talk about called the Museum Digital Backbone.
So Biodiversity Heritage Library basically encompasses almost the
totality of the sum of digitized literature that we have.
Of course, it's not complete because it very much is focused on that heritage
literature, but it's been a great place to start.
And those of you who saw Hiris Ghu's presentation earlier this
week will have seen how we're basically trying to build a new
discovery layer for BHL, which extracts
institutional names, taxa, specimens, chunks,
articles,
and we're working closely with Mistral, who have--
We've ReOSI-ed almost the entirety of BHL now, and we
are extracting those entities. And this is forming the
backbone for what we call the literature layer of
the planetary knowledge base.
Another big, very practical problem that we have, and one actually that
you're going to be hearing about from Ariana very shortly,
is how do we digitize at scale and extract and
transcribe all the entities that we have in
our things like our card indexes, our specimen labels, our
herbarium sheets, where much of that information resides in
analog form. I won't spoil the surprise of what
Ariana's going to be talking about next, but just to say that
Scribe has been our solution to that.
And again, this is helping us with that knowledge extraction piece for the
planetary knowledge base.
And then the last thing, and those of you who are invested in big
institutions like me at the Natural History Museum in London, there's always
a challenge of how do you deliver institutional value on these
projects. It's not just about core research, it's about how can we deliver
value closer to home. And one of the things is we sit on
vast repositories of data that sometimes we can't
share, in some cases for very good reasons.
Things like grant proposals, for example.
Things like the archive of publications that our scientists have
built. And so we've been building something we call the Museum Digital
Backbone, which is essentially a sort of miniaturized
version of this knowledge graph and LLM.
We've actually tried to accelerate it using a tool out of the box called
Amazon Quick, which is sort of designed to help
institutions and organizations do this thing very quickly.
And we're using it to help pull data for
publications, to pull data for writing grants,
to help our own scientists accelerate their research internally.
So the overall architecture of this is,
we're now just at the point where we're starting to think about all these different
layers taking us from that source evidence to those series of
services. But mindful of time, I just want to focus on a few
key design principles. And one that's been absolutely central
to this vision is how we track attribution and benefits
through that value chain from source evidence right the way
through to the services that we build.
And then how do we return that value to the communities that
have actually proportionately contributed to it?
And this has led to a series of literally
design principles that are kind of baked into our thinking about how we
deliver this. So critically, we want to preserve those
evidence layers at every step by basically making use
of all the identifiers, all of the provenance, all of the
licenses that are baked into that data.
We want to proportionally make all the contributions that people have
made to
surfacing these datasets. We want to make that visible through
attribution, and then we want to share those benefits And
maybe most controversially of all, we want to look at
what remuneration models might be appropriate to deliver
those benefits back to the wider community.
The ambition here is not that we're building some infrastructure just
for one institution. This is very much a vision for a
global infrastructure which is community led.
We have a series of use cases that I'm running out of time, I think, to go
into deeply, but particular areas of interest are actually
around biodiversity change. So how do we synthesize metrics from
all of this data that track that change?
And also, how do we use those commercially to generate revenue?
We have some examples of that already within the Natural History Museum with the
Biodiversity Intactness Index that we work with Bloomberg
to literally sell that data source to.
But we're trying to use the planetary knowledge base of the sort of tooling that
we're building to accelerate the production of those metrics.
We're also looking at areas like big pharma, which have a deep
interest in our data, but also, quite controversially,
have
not necessarily particularly strong sort of ethical practices.
So we're trying to work with them. And then I'll wrap up now because I can see our
moderator has stood up. Really just to acknowledge the fact that there are many
people working on this,
and there's a whole team behind it, but also to emphasize we're hiring
a new AI engineer at the moment. So if you're interested in coming to the museum
and working on this, do come and talk to me. Thanks for your time.
